opus-5.5.text:
I think they're closely related, but they're not the same thing. You could say agent RL is a natural extension of the reasoning-style RL we've been doing.

With strong-thinking RL, the core idea is that the model learns to use more test-time compute to think. It produces a long chain of thought, tries different approaches, reflects, backtracks, and finally gives an answer. But this is mostly a single-turn process. The model is basically talking to itself, and the environment is pretty static. You give it a math problem or a coding problem, it thinks, and then you check whether the answer is right.

Agent RL takes this one step further. The model isn't only thinking inside its own head anymore. It interacts with an external environment over many turns. It calls tools, runs code, searches, reads the results, and then decides what to do next based on the feedback. So in a sense, the thinking gets externalized. Part of the reasoning now happens through actions in the world, not only through tokens in the context.

From a technical perspective, a lot of the infrastructure and methodology carries over. You still need a good reward signal, you still need to scale up the rollouts, and you still care about things like long context and stability during training. But agent RL brings new challenges. The trajectories are much longer, the environment can be slow or nondeterministic, and the credit assignment gets harder because you take many steps before you know whether the task succeeded. You also have to build lots of realistic environments, which is a big engineering effort in itself.

So the way I see it, strong-thinking RL taught the model how to think deeply, and agent RL teaches the model how to act on that thinking to actually get things done. I believe the second one is closer to what we eventually want, which is a model that can independently complete long, complex tasks. Thinking is the foundation, and agency is where the real value gets unlocked.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're really two sides of the same thing, and the way I'd put it is that strong thinking is the foundation, and agents are what that foundation becomes once you connect it to the outside world.

When we talk about reinforcement learning for thinking, what you're really training is the model's ability to run a long, self-corrected chain of reasoning inside its own head. It learns to plan, to verify, to notice when it's wrong and back up. That skill is mostly internal. The reward signal is whether the final answer is right, and the model figures out on its own that spending more compute on reasoning gets it there more often.

Agent reinforcement learning takes that same loop and extends it outward. Now the chain of thought doesn't just stay in the model. It gets interrupted by actions: calling a tool, running code, searching, reading a document, and then the environment talks back. The model has to fold that feedback into its reasoning and keep going. So structurally it's the same optimization, but the trajectory is now a mix of thinking and acting, and the horizon is much longer.

The reason I say thinking comes first is that if a model can't reason reliably over a long internal chain, it definitely can't do it when the chain is being perturbed by noisy external observations. Agent tasks are strictly harder. Every tool call is a chance to go off track. A model with weak reasoning will take an action, get an unexpected result, and just drift. A model with strong reasoning treats that result as new evidence and replans.

There's also a nice feedback effect going the other way. Once you train on agentic environments, the reasoning itself gets better, because the world gives you much richer and more honest reward signals than a static dataset does. Did the code run? Did the test pass? Did you actually find the information? Those are hard to fake, so the model learns to think in a more grounded way. So I don't see them as sequential stages so much as a flywheel: better thinking enables longer, more reliable agent behavior, and real environments produce the training signal that makes the thinking better.

The practical difference for us as a lab is mostly in infrastructure. Thinking RL is about scaling the length and quality of reasoning within a single forward pass, so the challenge is things like long-context efficiency and reward design. Agent RL is about building environments, handling many steps, dealing with sparse and delayed rewards, and making sure the model generalizes across tools rather than memorizing one. That's a lot more engineering, but the underlying principle hasn't changed. You're still just letting the model discover, through trial and feedback, how to spend compute to get the right outcome.

r001.rationale: The response describes internal reasoning and external agent actions as related forms of reinforcement learning, but it does not identify both as ways of scaling token usage at prediction time.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re closely related. Strong-thinking reinforcement learning focuses on how a model reasons: can it break down a problem, explore possible solutions, check its work, and arrive at a better answer? Agent reinforcement learning extends that process to interaction with an environment. The model takes an action, gets feedback, and decides what to do next.

The common problem is learning to make a sequence of decisions that leads to a good outcome. Thinking is part of that sequence, and so are actions like calling a tool. For an agent, the question becomes: should I think more with the information I have, or take an action to get new information?

But better reasoning doesn’t automatically produce a better agent. An agent also has to deal with failed actions, incomplete observations, and rewards that may come much later. Those capabilities need training in an interactive setting.

So I see strong thinking as an important foundation for agents, while agent reinforcement learning brings reasoning into a broader loop of action and feedback. Ultimately, you want to optimize that whole loop together.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re closely connected. Strong-thinking reinforcement learning mainly trains a model to reason through a problem before giving an answer. Agent reinforcement learning expands that process: the model can take actions, use tools, observe what happens, and adjust its next step.

You can view both as learning to make a sequence of decisions. In one case, the steps are mostly internal reasoning; in the other, they also involve interaction with an environment. The underlying objective is similar: learn which sequence of decisions leads to a better outcome.

The important difference is feedback. For a reasoning problem, you may be able to check the final answer fairly easily. For an agent doing a long task, success can depend on many actions, and feedback may arrive much later. That makes exploration and figuring out which actions contributed to success more difficult.

So I see strong reasoning as an important foundation for agents, but not a substitute for training them through interaction. Ultimately, I think the two will converge: a model should learn when to think more, when to act, and when to use feedback to revise its plan.
